newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian businesman enmeshed in U.S. campaign.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian businesman enmeshed in U.S. campaign.

text.p: James Riady, deputy chairman of Indonesia's Lippo group and a member of one of the country's wealthiest families, has been caught up in the U.S. election campaign through his friendship with President Bill Clinton.

Republicans waging an uphill battle for the presidency have questioned donations to Clinton's Democratic Party from people connected to the Lippo group, suggesting the aim was to influence U.S. government policy.
The Los Angeles Times said on Wednesday that Riady, his family and executives of their companies had contributed $475,000 to the Democratic Party and its candidates since 1991.
The White House has denied any impropriety linked to the contributions and Riady has not commented on the reports.

The Lippo group, with interests ranging from banking, insurance and securities to property, trading and health care, has operations and offices in several Asian countries, Australia and the United States.
James Riady, 39, one of three sons of Lippo founder Mochtar Riady, himself the son of Chinese immigrants, is the dapper head of the group's Indonesian operations.
He graduated in accountancy and economics from Australia's Melbourne University in 1977, and afterwards served an internship with the Irving Trust and Investment Bank in Little Rock, Arkansas.
Clinton was state attorney-general at the time and, according to biographical reports, that is when Riady first met him.
Riady returned to Little Rock to help run Lippo's then-owned Arkansas-based Worthen Bank and Trust in the mid-1980s when Clinton was state governor, reviving their friendship.
Riady was one of the few non-Americans invited to an economic summit held by Clinton shortly before his inauguration as president in 1992.

Business sources said Lippo was well connected through the "bamboo" network of ethnic Chinese businessmen in Asia, although it is not regarded as close to President Suharto's influential family within Indonesia.

"Only a few Indonesians have a vision about their country. James is one of the few who has a vision about the country and the company," a top executive in a rival firm, who asked not to be named, told Reuters.

Analyst Jusuf Wanandi said however that James Riady's flamboyant style did not sit well with all Indonesians and could attract criticism from those opposed to the dominant commercial interests of the ethnic Chinese minority in the country.
Diplomatic sources in Jakarta said there seemed to be nothing illegal in the donations to the Democratic Party, which appeared to have been made openly and transparently.
A senior Indonesian economist, who asked not to be named, described the amount as "peanuts", and said he disagreed with the perception that Riady was an Indonesian lobbyist in the United States.
